title: The AI code wars are heating up
description: The Verge examines the intensifying competition between OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to build the best AI coding tools, even as developers express fears about AI coding tools. The article questions which model actually writes the best code and references the 'Claude Code Moment' from early 2026.
author: The Verge

title: Claude Token Counter, now with model comparisons
description: Simon Willison upgraded his Claude Token Counter tool to compare tokenization between Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.6. Key finding: Opus 4.7 uses a new tokenizer that can increase token count by 1.0-1.35× depending on content type. For system prompts, the increase was 1.46×. For images, up to 3.01× (due to higher resolution support: 2,576 pixels vs prior models). The token inflation makes Opus 4.7 around 40% more expensive at the same per-token pricing.
author: Simon Willison

title: Headless everything for personal AI
description: Matt Webb and others predict that 'headless' services (API-only, no GUI) will become much more common as personal AI agents interact with services directly rather than through bot-controlled browser automation. Salesforce announced 'Salesforce Headless 360' exposing everything as APIs, MCP, & CLI. This trend could disrupt per-seat SaaS pricing models since AI agents don't need GUIs.
author: Simon Willison (citing Matt Webb, Marc Benioff, Brandur Leach)

title: Changes in the system prompt between Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7
description: Simon analyzed Anthropic's published system prompts (unique transparency among AI labs) and documented changes between Opus 4.6 and 4.7. He also created a git timeline of all Claude system prompts back to July 2024 using Claude Code to convert the archive into separate files with fake git commit dates for browsing evolution via GitHub's commit view.
author: Simon Willison

title: Datasette 1.0a28: fixes using Claude Code and Opus 4.7
description: Simon released Datasette 1.0a28 to fix compatibility bugs introduced in 1.0a27. Notably, 'Most of the changes in this release were implemented using Claude Code and the newly released Claude Opus 4.7.' Shows practical use of AI coding tools for maintenance work.
author: Simon Willison

title: Claude Opus 4.7 announced by Anthropic
description: Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.7 on April 16, 2026. Key improvements: 3x better resolution on Rakuten-SWE-Bench production tasks vs Opus 4.6; SWE-bench Verified: 87.6%, SWE-bench Pro: 64.3%; first Claude model with high-resolution image support (2576px / 3.75MP); better at code quality, test quality, financial analysis, and data visualization. Available in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, Cursor, and GitHub. Same pricing ($5/$25) but new tokenizer increases real cost by up to 35%.
author: Anthropic

title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B vs Claude Opus 4.7: pelican benchmark
description: Simon compared the newly released Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from Alibaba against Claude Opus 4.7 using his notorious 'pelican riding a bicycle' image generation benchmark. The local Qwen model running on his laptop produced a better pelican than the frontier Claude model. Demonstrates how open/local models are catching up in certain visual generation tasks.
author: Simon Willison

title: llm-anthropic 0.25: Claude Opus 4.7 support with thinking_effort
description: Release of llm-anthropic 0.25 adding support for Claude Opus 4.7, which includes the new 'thinking_effort': 'xhigh' parameter. Also adds 'thinking_display' and 'thinking_adaptive' boolean options, and increases default max_tokens to the maximum allowed for each model.
author: Simon Willison

title: Parasail raises $32M to feed 'tokenmaxxing' AI developers
description: Parasail, a cloud computing service for AI model inference, raised $32M Series A. The company generates 500 billion tokens daily and rents processing time at 40 data centers in 15 countries. The investment signals a fractured future where developers use hybrid architectures: open models for initial screening to drive down costs, then frontier models for final answers. Andreas Stuhlmüller (Elicit CEO) noted they've moved to open models because sending 100,000s of requests to API endpoints is 'pretty rough.' Samir Kumar (Touring Capital) expects inference to be at least 20% of software development costs.
author: Tim Fernholz

title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS: prompt-directed text-to-speech
description: Google released Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, a text-to-speech model that can be directed using elaborate prompts. The prompting guide is surprisingly detailed, with example prompts that include extensive 'AUDIO PROFILE' and 'DIRECTOR'S NOTES' sections specifying style, dynamics, pace, and accent. Simon vibe-coded a UI to try it out with multi-speaker conversation support.
author: Simon Willison

title: Datasette 1.0a27: CSRF protection revolution
description: Major Datasette update replacing Django-style CSRF tokens with modern Sec-Fetch-Site header protection, following Filippo Valsorda's research that shipped in Go 1.25. Removes all <input type='hidden' name='csrftoken'> from templates. Also adds RenameTableEvent for plugins to react to table renames, new actor= parameter for client methods, and Database(is_temp_disk=True) option.
author: Simon Willison

title: Andrej Karpathy's 'Slopacolypse' and AI coding shift
description: Andrej Karpathy coined the term 'Slopacolypse' for 2026, reflecting concerns about AI-generated content quality. He reports that AI is now writing most of his code, leading him to feel his own coding abilities are atrophying. Karpathy describes a dramatic shift from 80% manual+autocomplete coding and 20% agents to the opposite, with AI agents now doing the majority of coding work. He calls this 'vibe coding' - a fundamental transformation in how developers work. By early 2026, 51% of all code committed to GitHub was either generated or substantially assisted by AI.
author: Andrej Karpathy

title: Replace token-based CSRF with Sec-Fetch-Site header protection
description: Simon landed a major PR replacing Datasette's CSRF token protection with modern Sec-Fetch-Site header protection, following research by Filippo Valsorda. Claude Code did much of the work across 10 commits, closely guided by Simon and cross-reviewed by GPT-5.4. However, Simon decided to write the PR description by hand 'as an exercise in keeping myself honest.'
author: Simon Willison

title: OpenAI GPT-5.4-Cyber: response to Claude Mythos
description: OpenAI announced GPT-5.4-Cyber, a cyber-permissive variant fine-tuned for defensive cybersecurity use cases, as their answer to Claude Mythos. They also extended their 'Trusted Access for Cyber' program requiring government ID verification for 'reduced friction' access. Simon notes the announcement is difficult to follow and doesn't mention Anthropic, but still requires a Google Form application for the best tools.
author: Simon Willison

title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now
description: The UK's AI Safety Institute published an evaluation of Claude Mythos's cyber capabilities. Drew Breunig noted that the more tokens (money) spent, the better the security results. This creates an economic equation: 'to harden a system you need to spend more tokens discovering exploits than attackers will spend exploiting them.' This makes open source libraries MORE valuable since tokens spent securing them are shared across all users, countering the vibe-coding replacement narrative.
author: Simon Willison (citing Drew Breunig, AISI)

title: Claude Opus 4.7 discussions on Hacker News
description: Hacker News threads discussed Claude Opus 4.7's release, with technical comparisons between Opus 4.6 and 4.7 tokenizer costs, and community reactions to the new model's capabilities and pricing. Users debated the token inflation issue and shared experiences with the new model.
author: Hacker News Community

title: Claude Opus 4.7 tokenizer cost discussions
description: Hacker News discussion measuring Claude 4.7's tokenizer costs, with references to military use cases and comparisons of token efficiency between versions. Users shared benchmarks and analyzed the economic impact of the new tokenizer.
author: Hacker News Community
